paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A cavernous open mouth, a long sigh – yawning is a common human response, especially to an experience that is dull, uneventful or tiring. But surprisingly little is known about the mechanisms underlying this behaviour, commonly associated with tedium or boredom. Scientists have known for decades that yawns can be infectious, so much so that seeing another person yawn can trigger a series of gaping mouths in what is known as 'contagious yawning', but again, there have been few empirical studies to explain this phenomenon. Now, recent research at the University of Albany in the US suggests a basic explanation for yawning, and two studies in the UK, one at the University of Leeds and the other at the University of London, have explored contagious yawning.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: It has been theorised for some time that yawning increases oxygen levels in the brain, helping to maintain alertness. This could explain why yawning is often seen when people are waiting for something stressful to happen, such as athletes just before an event. However, in the Albany research, Dr Andrew Gallop and his colleagues concluded that people do not yawn because they need oxygen. The experiments, using college students as subjects, showed that raising or lowering oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood failed to produce yawning. Rather, Dr Gallop argues as an interpretation of his experimental results, yawning acts as a brain-cooling mechanism. Our brains, not unlike computers, operate more efficiently when cool, and yawning enhances the brain's functioning by increasing the blood flow and drawing in fresh air. To test this theory, the Albany researchers asked individual volunteers to watch a video showing people behaving neutrally, laughing or yawning. Observers watching through a one-way mirror counted how many times the volunteers yawned in reaction. Some volunteers were asked to inhale only through their noses as they watched. Later volunteers were asked to press warm or cold packs on their foreheads while looking at the videos. The two conditions thought to promote brain cooling (nasal inhalation and forehead cooling) practically eliminated yawning amongst the volunteers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Many animals, including fish, birds, cats and crocodiles, yawn spontaneously; however, only some humans, chimpanzees, and possibly macaque monkeys yawn infectiously – that is when seeing another do so. Sometimes just reading about or thinking about yawning triggers a yawning reaction among people. Previous studies found that between 40 and 60 per cent of adult humans subconsciously copy others when they yawn. And another earlier study found that the same area near the back of the human brain is activated during both infectious yawning and during feelings of empathy (or sympathy) with other people.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The University of Leeds study attempted to show conclusively the link between contagious yawning and empathy. Dr Catriona Morrison, a cognitive psychologist, carried out an experiment involving 40 psychology students and 40 engineering students. As Dr Morrison explained, 'We worked with psychologists because they are regarded as more empathetic, and engineers because they are often seen as mostly interested in objects and functions and systems.' The students, half of whom were male and half female, were made to sit in a small room facing a person who had been instructed to yawn 10 times in 10 minutes. The volunteers (who believed they were waiting for an experiment to start) were unaware that they were being monitored. On average the engineers yawned 1.5 times and the psychologists 5.5 times. The researchers concluded that a higher degree of empathy and more frequent infectious yawning are directly associated. Dr Morrison and her colleagues were surprised to find that while women are usually considered more empathetic than men, the statistics proved to be very similar across all participants.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Another insight into the reason for yawning being infectious has come from the University of London work, which focused on observing 24 boys and girls with autism, and a matching control group of 25 non-autistic children. Generally, autistic people do not display empathy towards others and they are usually unable to form normal emotional ties with people they live with. Dr Atsushi Senju, the leader of the research team, reported that the autistic children in his experiments did yawn spontaneously as often as the non-autistic children. However, they were not as susceptible to infectious yawning as the non-autistic children. When shown pre-recorded tapes of adults yawning, the control group of children yawned significantly more than did the children with autism.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of these recent studies explains conclusively why yawning occurs at all or why it should have evolved into an involuntary reaction for people. You don't have to learn how to yawn and you don't choose to yawn. It just happens. One theory is that it has something to do with the fact that humans once lived in groups and that infectious yawning was important to bond people together. Or it may have simply indicated, 'I need rest. You stay awake for now.' In other words, it helped to raise alertness levels and therefore helped groups to remain vigilant when danger was close. It would thus have arisen through evolution as a basic method of non-verbal communication among early men.

groups.title: How yawning may have evolved
content: Infectious yawning may have developed as a way to {{23}} individuals into a tighter social unit. Alternatively, it may have been used to increase alertness during times of {{24}} . For example, yawning might have signalled that someone wanted a period of {{25}} and required another member of the group to remain vigilant. So yawning might have been part of a simple {{26}} system used by early humans.
